query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailor the HVAF‐i7 torch’s gas preheat temperature using a thermal model specific to FeCoNiCrAl to raise the in‐flight particle temperature just enough for optimal partial melting and splat coalescence.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy alloy feedstock (15–45 μm) that when sprayed using standard HVAF-i7 settings yields acceptable surface quality but insufficient coating thickness.
generation.intervention: Increase the HVAF‐i7 combustion gas preheat temperature by a calculated increment based on the alloy’s melting point, specific heat, and thermal diffusivity. This requires first performing a quantitative thermal analysis of FeCoNiCrAl to determine the ideal preheat setting that maximizes melting without triggering extra oxidation.
generation.conditions: Deposition under an inert atmosphere (as currently used) on substrates including confined geometries (internal diameters as small as 120 mm) with all other parameters held constant.
generation.structural_mediator: A higher in‐flight particle temperature promotes improved particle melting, leading to better splat flattening and rapid inter-splat bonding. The controlled extra heat minimizes incomplete melting while avoiding overheating-induced oxidation.
generation.mechanism: FeCoNiCrAl’s high melting point and modest thermal conductivity require extra in-flight energy to achieve a liquid-like impact state. A tailored increment in gas preheat increases the particle’s thermal energy absorption as they fly toward the substrate, thus improving melting and forming wider, more adherent splats. This enhanced local consolidation builds up coating thickness more effectively while keeping as-sprayed oxidation levels low in an inert environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in coating thickness by approximately 25–40% relative to the 15–45 μm baseline is expected, with maintained or improved adhesion and minimal oxidation.
generation.baseline: Coatings deposited using the standard HVAF‐i7 torch gas preheat setting and 15–45 μm feedstock.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective if the increased gas preheat temperature remains within limits that prevent complete melting/excessive oxidation and does not compromise deposition uniformity in confined geometries.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal temperature increment for FeCoNiCrAl needs calibration; predictions on thickness increase are approximate until validated against detailed thermal profiling.

HVAF coating technology is the combustion of propane in a compressed air stream. Like HVOF, this produces a uniform high velocity jet. HVAF differs by including a heat baffle to further stabilize the thermal spray mechanisms. Material is injected into the air-fuel stream and coating particles are propelled toward the part. HVAF has a maximum flame temperature of 3,560° to 3,650 °F and an average particle velocity of 3,300 ft/sec. Since the maximum flame temperature is relatively close to the melting point of most spray materials, HVAF results in a more uniform, ductile coating. This also allows for a typical coating thickness of 0.002–0.050". HVAF coatings also have a mechanical bond strength of greater that 12,000 psi. Common HVAF coating materials include, but are not limited to; tungsten carbide, chrome carbide, stainless steel, hastelloy, and inconel. Due to its ductile nature hvaf coatings can help resist cavitation damage.

papers.title: In-situ CrFeCoNi medium entropy alloying coating via electrospark powder deposition.

verdicts.fix: Incorporate material-specific thermal and oxidation data for FeCoNiCrAl in HVAF conditions to define an optimal particle velocity range and better justify how a nozzle redesign benefits the deposition without adverse side effects.

paper_did: Developed an in‐situ CrFeCoNi medium entropy alloy coating on A516 steel using electrospark powder deposition (ESPD) with a slurry of Cr, Fe, Co, and Ni powders.

Optimized deposition parameters (capacitance, voltage, pulse frequency) to achieve nearly equiatomic composition and controlled melting, addressing issues such as incomplete melting and tungsten contamination.
Employed a dual deposition process (combining ESPD and electrospark deposition of electrode material for surface smoothening) to improve coating morphology.
Characterized the coating’s microstructure (using OM, SEM/EDX, XRD, EBSD), measured microhardness, and performed wear tests to evaluate the mechanical performance.
paper_reported: The formation of a nearly equiatomic CrFeCoNi coating exhibiting an FCC phase with columnar grain structure and a microhardness of approximately 331.5 ± 18.9 HV.
A significant improvement in wear resistance with a 95.56% reduction in the specific wear rate relative to the bare A516 steel substrate.
Observations that deposition energy input is critical: low energy can lead to incomplete melting (e.g., unmelted Co and Ni), whereas excessive energy results in electrode (W) contamination.
paper_proposed: That the powder‐based electrospark deposition technique can be extended to in‐situ M/HEA coatings using arbitrary element combinations for tailored properties.
Further investigation into the influence of powder morphology and additional process parameter optimization to improve coating quality.
Exploration of dual deposition (ESPD combined with a secondary, lower-energy re-melting step) as a method to smoothen the coating surface and enhance metallurgical bonding.

paper_did: Prepared high‐entropy coatings using commercial gas‐atomized AlCoCrFeNi powder (average particle size ~20 μm) via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) onto Ni-based alloy substrates.

Subjected the as-sprayed coatings to isothermal oxidation treatments at temperatures of 650 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, and 1000 °C for various durations (20 h, 50 h, 100 h—with one instance mentioned at 200 h) in a tube furnace.

Characterized the coatings using X‐ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and image analysis (ImageJ) to document oxide formation, layer morphology, and phase transitions.
paper_reported: At the initial stages of oxidation a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure forms on the coating surface, which later develops into a two‐layer system with a top mixed-oxide layer and a bottom continuous Al2O3 layer.

Oxidation leads to significant elemental redistribution: Al diffuses toward the surface to form Al2O3 while an aluminum-poor layer develops underneath, triggering phase transitions in the coating matrix.

The internal microstructure evolves from the as-sprayed BCC/B2 mixture into a dual-phase structure consisting of Al–Ni-rich ordered B2 phases and Fe–Cr-rich disordered A2 (or FCC) phases; the mechanisms are attributed to selective oxidation of Al and associated atomic diffusion.
paper_proposed: Although not stated explicitly as a future work section, the paper highlights the incomplete understanding of high-temperature oxidation and phase transformation in APS-deposited AlCoCrFeNi coatings, implicitly suggesting that further work is needed to optimize oxidation resistance and to fully unravel the diffusion-driven phase evolution.

There is an implied need for exploring modifications in processing parameters (e.g., spray conditions, thermal treatments) to improve the protective performance of high-entropy coatings in high-temperature applications.

paper_did: Prepared high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coatings using FeCoNiCrMo0.2 powder on 316L stainless steel by laser cladding.

Modified the base HEA by adding various amounts of WC (from 8% up to 40%) and identified that a 32% WC addition yielded an optimal trade‐off between hardness improvement and acceptable coating morphology.
Further added 2% nano‐CeO2 to the FeCoNiCrMo0.2 + 32%WC composite to refine the grain structure, reduce porosity and cracking, and achieve a uniform hardness distribution.

Characterized the coatings by means of XRD (to reveal phase changes and carbide/intermetallic formation), SEM/EDS (to assess microstructure and elemental distribution), microhardness testing, wear (friction coefficient) evaluation, and corrosion testing.
paper_reported: The addition of WC significantly increases the microhardness (e.g., from 470.6 HV0.2 for pure HEA to ~562 HV0.2 for the HEA/WC coating) and improves wear resistance, although too high a WC content induces cracking and porosity.

Nano‐CeO2 addition (2%) refines the grain structure, suppresses the formation of complex carbide/intermetallic phases, reduces defects, and enhances corrosion resistance (higher polarization impedance and lower corrosion rate).

XRD analysis confirmed that while WC addition generates extra diffraction peaks (due to carbides and intermetallic compounds), the addition of CeO2 mitigates these changes to recover a phase pattern similar to the unalloyed HEA.
Element distribution studies (EDS) demonstrated that Ce accumulates at grain boundaries, contributing a pinning effect that leads to more uniform dispersion of the constituent elements.
paper_proposed: That the optimized composite coating (FeCoNiCrMo0.2 + 32%WC + 2%CeO2) offers the best overall performance in terms of hardness, wear, and corrosion resistance and can be used to extend the service life of 316L stainless steel.
That the experimental results and microstructural insights provide a theoretical and practical basis for further research into process optimization and property enhancement of HEA coatings.

paper_did: Prepared three types of coatings on 316L stainless steel by laser cladding: a pure FeCoNiCrMo0.2 high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating, a composite HEA + 32%WC coating, and a composite HEA + 32%WC + 2%CeO2 coating.

Modified the coating composition by adding WC powder to improve hardness and wear resistance, and further added nano‐CeO2 to refine the grain structure, reduce porosity and cracks, and stabilize hardness and friction behavior.

Carried out extensive characterization including macro and microstructural analysis (via optical microscopy, SEM, EDS), phase identification (XRD), microhardness measurements, wear tests, and electrochemical corrosion tests.
paper_reported: The addition of WC significantly increased the hardness and wear resistance of the HEA coating, but also led to uneven distribution of the hard phases and introduced some porosity.

Incorporating 2% nano‐CeO2 refined the grain structure (by grain boundary pinning), reduced porosity and cracking, and produced a more uniform hardness distribution with improved corrosion resistance compared to the WC‐only coating.
The optimized composite coating (FeCoNiCrMo0.2 + 32%WC + 2%CeO2) displayed the best overall performance, suggesting its potential to extend the service life of 316L stainless steel components.

paper_did: Developed NiCoCrAlFe high entropy alloy coatings by thermally spraying equiatomic elemental powders (Ni, Co, Cr, Al, Fe) on SS316L substrates after ball‐milling for homogeneous mixing.
Applied an annealing treatment at 1000 °C for 4 hours in an inert atmosphere to promote atomic diffusion and the formation of a uniform HEA solid solution.

Characterized the as‐sprayed and annealed coatings using SEM (for splat and lamellar morphology), EDS (for elemental mapping), XRD (for phase identification of BCC, FCC, and oxide phases), micro-Vickers hardness, surface roughness testing, and potentiodynamic corrosion assessments in a 3.5% NaCl medium.
paper_reported: The as‐sprayed coatings exhibited a splat morphology with a mix of BCC and FCC phases along with some oxidized regions; annealing enhanced atomic diffusion, increasing the fraction of the white solid solution phase with reduced free metal and oxide content.
Annealed coatings showed a lamellar microstructure with enhanced homogenization and lower microhardness (due to reduced dislocations) compared to the as‐sprayed state.

Potentiodynamic corrosion tests demonstrated that the annealed coatings produced a significantly lower corrosion current density (Icorr) and a more pronounced passive region, indicating improved corrosion resistance over both as‐sprayed coatings and the bare SS316L substrate.
paper_proposed: The paper proposes the potential application of these annealed HEA coatings as corrosion‐resistant protective layers for stainless steel, especially for use in chloride-rich environments, but does not delve into further process parameter optimizations.

paper_did: Synthesized NiCoCrAlFe high entropy alloy (HEA) coatings by ball‐milling elemental powders (Ni, Co, Cr, Al, Fe) in equal‐atomic ratios.
Deposited coatings onto stainless steel 316L substrates using atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) with pre-treated (cleaned, grit-blasted, flame pre-heated) substrates.
Conducted a post-deposition annealing at 1000 °C for 4 hours in an inert atmosphere to promote elemental diffusion and formation of a solid-solution HEA.

Characterized the as-sprayed and annealed coatings by SEM (including cross-sectional and microstructural analysis), XRD (phase identification of BCC and FCC phases), micro Vickers hardness, surface roughness measurements, and potentiodynamic polarization corrosion testing in 3.5% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: The as-sprayed coatings exhibited a lamellar, splat-type microstructure with some oxide phases and partially melted particles, indicating incomplete alloy formation during deposition.

Annealing significantly enhanced elemental diffusion, increasing the fraction of the white (fully alloyed HEA) phase and yielding a mixed BCC/FCC structure with improved homogeneity and reduced porosity.

After annealing, the coatings demonstrated lower microhardness (due to reduced dislocation density), lower surface roughness, and markedly enhanced corrosion resistance compared to both the as-sprayed coating and bare stainless steel 316L.
paper_proposed: While no explicit future experimental intervention was laid out, the study implied that further optimization of the HEA coating fabrication (e.g., improved deposition techniques, process management to control oxidation and microstructure) could render these coatings strong candidates as protective layers against chloride-induced corrosion.

A coating of about 1-200 µm can reduce the temperature at the superalloy surface by up to 200 K. HVAF differs by including a heat baffle to further stabilize the thermal spray mechanisms. Material is injected into the air-fuel stream and coating particles are propelled toward the part. Thermal spraying techniques are coating processes in which melted (or heated) materials are sprayed onto a surface. The "feedstock" (coating precursor) is heated by electrical (plasma or arc) or chemical means (combustion flame). The bond coat is an oxidation-resistant metallic layer which is deposited directly on top of the metal substrate. It is typically 75-150 μm thick and made of a NiCrAlY or NiCoCrAlY alloy, though other bond coats made of Ni and Pt aluminides also exist. A powder mixture of metal and normal glass can be plasma-sprayed in vacuum, with a suitable composition resulting in a TBC comparable to YSZ. Additionally, metal-glass composites have superior bond-coat adherence, higher thermal expansion coefficients, and no open porosity, which prevents oxidation of the bond-coat.

paper_did: Manufactured thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems on Nimonic 75 substrates by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using a NiCrAlY bond coat (with inherent inter‐lamellar porosities) and a nanostructured yttria‐stabilized zirconia top coat.
Conducted long‐term isothermal oxidation tests at 1150 °C (in eight cycles totaling 800 h) as well as cyclic thermal shock tests at 1200 °C and 1250 °C.

Characterized the microstructure and interface of the coatings – including TGO formation, porosity evolution, sintering/densification effects, and adhesion differences – via SEM, EDS, image analysis, and scratch testing.
paper_reported: The inter‐lamellar porosities in the bond coat promoted the formation and distribution of the thermally grown oxide (TGO) over a larger area, which helped control TGO thickness and deter spallation.

During long‐term oxidation, fine cracks appeared in the top ceramic coat at 400 h and evolved into larger cracks by 800 h while densification of both the ceramic and bond coat occurred, yet the overall adhesion remained high.
Under thermal shock conditions the nanostructured system withstood 1242 cycles at 1200 °C and 555 cycles at 1250 °C, with damage mainly confined to the ceramic top coat.
paper_proposed: Performing future studies to assess the effect of different bond coat porosity levels on traditional TBCs and related environmental coatings.
Extending investigations to evaluate the corrosion resistance of thermal barrier coatings that utilize a less‐dense bond coat.

HVAF differs by including a heat baffle to further stabilize the thermal spray mechanisms. Material is injected into the air-fuel stream and coating particles are propelled toward the part. The bond coat is an oxidation-resistant metallic layer which is deposited directly on top of the metal substrate. It is typically 75-150 μm thick and made of a NiCrAlY or NiCoCrAlY alloy, though other bond coats made of Ni and Pt aluminides also exist. The primary purpose of the bond coat is to protect the metal substrate from oxidation and corrosion, particularly from oxygen and corrosive element

A powder mixture of metal and normal glass can be plasma-sprayed in vacuum, with a suitable composition resulting in a TBC comparable to YSZ. Additionally, metal-glass composites have superior bond-coat adherence, higher thermal expansion coefficients, and no open porosity, which prevents oxidation of the bond-coat.

The bond coat adheres the thermal barrier to the substrate. Additionally, the bond coat provides oxidation protection and functions as a diffusion barrier against the motion of substrate atoms towards the environment. paper_did: Used AISI 304L steel substrates and prepared two sets: one directly pack‐aluminized and another first nickel‐electrodeposited then pack‐aluminized followed by diffusion annealing.

Performed high‐temperature oxidation (700–1100 °C for 8 h) to study oxide formation, mass gain, surface roughness, and degree of spallation, and evaluated microstructure and phase formation via SEM-EDS, XRD, optical microscopy and scratch testing.
Carried out hot corrosion tests using a Na2SO4 + NaCl salt mixture to compare the performance of the bare, as‐aluminized, and electrodeposited‐aluminized samples.
paper_reported: Direct aluminizing on AISI 304L did not yield a true aluminide coating but resulted in a nearly pure aluminum (or aluminum alloy) layer.
Nickel electrodeposition prior to aluminizing enabled the formation of a characteristic β–NiAl coating with minimal substrate element migration and excellent adhesion.

Oxidation studies revealed formation of transient oxides (θ–Al2O3 and NiAl2O4) at lower temperatures that converted to stable α–Al2O3 at higher temperatures, with increased surface roughness and spallation at the highest temperatures.
The electrodeposited–aluminized samples showed superior hot corrosion resistance relative to the others.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests that further improvements in coating performance may be achieved by incorporating reactive or noble elements into the aluminide to reduce the degree of spallation (DoS) and enhance high-temperature durability.

hypotheses.mechanism: A shorter stand-off distance minimizes the time particles spend in the flame, leading to a higher residual velocity and lower oxidation rate at deposition. paper_did: Prepared AISI 304L stainless steel samples by two routes: one set was directly aluminized via a high‐activity pack aluminizing process, and the other was first nickel–electrodeposited (using a Watts bath) followed by pack aluminizing and diffusion annealing.
Subjected the coated samples to isothermal oxidation at temperatures ranging from 700 °C to 1100 °C for 8 hours, followed by hot corrosion tests using a Na2SO4–NaCl salt mixture.

Utilized multiple characterization techniques (SEM-EDS, optical microscopy, XRD, scratch adhesion tests, surface roughness measurements, and weight change evaluation) to assess the microstructure, phase composition, adhesion, degree of spallation, and oxidation behavior of the coatings.
paper_reported: Direct aluminizing of AISI 304L (without a prior nickel coating) did not form a true aluminide layer but instead produced a nearly pure aluminum (or alloy) coating.

Nickel-electrodeposited substrates yielded a characteristic β-NiAl aluminide coating with a bilayer structure (a coating zone with an interdiffusion layer) and excellent adhesion (evidenced by a scratch test showing no cracking at 10 N and a critical load of 20 N).

Oxidation studies revealed a temperature-dependent phase evolution—from the formation of transient θ-Al2O3 and NiAl2O4 at lower temperatures to stable α-Al2O3 at temperatures between 1000 °C and 1100 °C—with concurrent increases in mass gain, surface roughness, and spallation; hot corrosion resistance was best for the electrodeposited-aluminized samples.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests further improvements to coating performance, specifically noting the need to enhance oxidation resistance (i.e., reduce the degree of spallation at high temperatures) by possibly incorporating reactive or noble elements into the aluminide system.
It hints at exploring modifications that would better balance diffusion and oxidation events, thus extending the coating’s service life under high-temperature and corrosive conditions.

This cleaner deposition process reduces the formation of oxide inclusions that can undermine the layer build‐up, thereby allowing thicker and more adherent coatings to be formed.

hypotheses.uncertainty: The net benefit in coating thickness and quality is dependent on the effectiveness of the shrouding design; quantitative improvements are not precisely predictable without experimental validation.

paper_did: Prepared AISI 304L steel substrates (cut, ground, and polished) and applied two processing routes: direct pack aluminizing and nickel electrodeposition followed by pack aluminizing and diffusion annealing.

Conducted pack aluminizing at 900 °C for 3 h, diffusion annealing at 1000 °C for 120 min in an argon atmosphere, and subsequent oxidation treatments (700–1100 °C for 8 h) as well as hot corrosion tests using a Na2SO4:NaCl (3:1 by weight) salt mixture.

Characterized microstructure, phase composition, adhesion (via scratch testing), degree of spallation, surface roughness, and oxidation behavior using SEM-EDS, XRD, optical microscopy, and weight-gain measurements.
paper_reported: Direct aluminizing on AISI 304L without prior nickel electroplating did not form a true aluminide coating but resulted in an almost pure aluminum (or alloy) layer.

Nickel electrodeposition prior to aluminizing produced a distinct β–NiAl layer with a bilayer structure (coating zone and interdiffusion zone), excellent adhesion, inhibited substrate element migration, and improved oxidation/hot corrosion performance.

Oxidation studies revealed that at lower temperatures (700–800 °C) transient oxides (θ–Al2O3 and NiAl2O4) formed, while higher temperatures (900–1100 °C) promoted conversion to stable α–Al2O3; however, higher temperatures also increased surface roughness and induced spallation.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests that incorporating reactive or noble elements into the aluminide coatings could further improve the degree of spallation (DoS) and high-temperature oxidation resistance.

paper_did: Synthesized an equimolar Cr‐Mn‐Fe‐Co high‐entropy alloy via 3D laser printing.
Performed high‐temperature oxidation experiments in synthetic air at 700 °C and 900 °C up to 48 hours with controlled heating and cooling cycles.

Characterized the alloy using weight‐gain measurements (to establish parabolic kinetics), X‐ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive spectroscopy to identify oxide phases and microstructural evolution.
paper_reported: The alloy’s oxidation behavior followed a parabolic rate law, with the parabolic rate constant increasing dramatically with temperature (e.g. from ~2.79 mg²/cm⁴/h at 700 °C to ~114 mg²/cm⁴/h at 900 °C).
Formation of mixed oxide phases such as MnFe₂O₄, MnFeO₂, Cr₂O₃, and spinel-type oxides was observed, and significant surface cracking and oxide spallation occurred at 900 °C.

The diffusion dynamics (inward oxygen and outward cation motion) and associated microstructural changes (e.g., void formation and matrix segmentation) were identified as key mechanisms affecting high‐temperature oxidation resistance.
paper_proposed: Based on the oxidation behavior findings, the paper suggests that the studied HEA appears more suitable for applications under 700 °C and implies that further work is needed to understand and mitigate the oxidation‐induced degradation (e.g., through compositional or microstructural modifications).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Reducing the spray (nozzle-to-substrate) distance to around 300–350 mm to increase particle velocity will increase deposition efficiency and produce a thicker, adherent FeCoNiCrAl bond coat.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with a 15–45 μm size distribution, as used in the current HVAF-i7 spray process.
hypotheses.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 torch process by reducing the spray distance (e.g., to 300–350 mm) and optimizing the fuel/air mixture to boost the in-flight particle velocity.
hypotheses.conditions: HVAF-i7 deposition in a configuration targeting internal diameters as small as 120 mm; deposition at temperatures relevant for high-temperature thermal-barrier service (typically under 700 °C conditions for bond coats) so that oxidation remains minimal.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic impact energy of particles produces improved flattening, bonding, and reduced in-flight deceleration, leading to better layer consolidation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases the momentum of the splats on impact, improves adhesion, and promotes greater deposition build-up per pass. The denser and better-flattened splats reduce porosity and limits the formation of premature oxide layers in-flight because they have shorter residence times in the heated environment.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Relative to coatings produced with the 15–45 μm feedstock at longer spray distances, the deposits will be significantly thicker (by an expected measurable gain; exact percent gain is uncertain) while retaining acceptable as-sprayed oxidation and bond integrity.
hypotheses.baseline: Coatings produced at the standard HVAF-i7 configuration with currently used spray distances which yield acceptable coating quality but limited thickness.
hypotheses.boundary: Effectiveness may be limited if the reduced distance causes excessive substrate heating or leads to overshooting the optimal particle melting state. The intervention must maintain the low oxidation conditions of the as-sprayed deposit.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimum reduction in distance may require fine-tuning; the precise magnitude of thickness improvement is not firmly predicted.

falsification_experiment.design: Deposit FeCoNiCrAl coatings using HVAF-i7 at the reduced spray distances (300–350 mm) while keeping other parameters constant versus a standard-distance control. Measure the coating thickness, porosity, oxidation content, and bond strength.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced spray distance does not produce a significant (>15–20%) increase in coating thickness without compromising oxidation levels or adhesion compared to the control, then the hypothesis is rejected.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the concept of spray-distance adjustment to increase particle velocity specifically in the HVAF-i7 process for FeCoNiCrAl HEA bond coats, addressing the thickness limitation while preserving oxidation resistance and adhesion.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Surface modification of the feedstock particles to introduce a thin, controlled oxide layer that enhances in-flight kinetic energy transfer will improve deposition efficiency and enable a thicker coating.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Commercially available FeCoNiCrAl powder (15–45 μm) used in HVAF-i7 processes, initially featuring a clean metallic surface.
hypotheses.intervention: Pre-treat the powder by a mild thermal oxidation step (or plasma pretreatment) to form a nanometer-scale oxide shell on the particles prior to spraying.
hypotheses.conditions: Deposition with the HVAF-i7 torch under standard conditions except for the use of modified powders; service conditions are the same high-temperature thermal-barrier environment as in conventional application.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The pre-formed oxide shell promotes localized softening and redeposition upon impact due to enhanced yield upon particle flattening, and it may reduce further excessive oxidation during flight.
hypotheses.mechanism: A nanometer-scale oxide layer can act to slightly lower the melting point at the particle surface and aid in better splat formation and coalescence upon impact. This improves inter-particle bonding and densification, resulting in increased net deposition per pass. Additionally, the initial oxide could serve as a barrier to further oxidation during flight, maintaining overall coating composition during deposition.

hypotheses.baseline: HVAF-i7 coatings produced with untreated 15–45 μm powder that exhibit inadequate thickness.
hypotheses.boundary: If the oxide layer is too thick, it may impair melting and splat formation; optimization is required. The intervention must not adversely affect the high-temperature service performance.
hypotheses.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal thickness and uniformity of the oxide shell to maximize the benefit without compromising oxidation resistance.

paper_did: Fabricated an equimolar Cr‐Mn‐Fe‐Co high-entropy alloy (HEA) using 3D laser printing from mixed Cr, Mn, Fe, and Co powders.
Performed high-temperature oxidation experiments in synthetic air at 700 °C and 900 °C for durations up to 48 hours.
Measured oxidation kinetics via mass gain analyses and characterized the oxidized samples using XRD, SEM, and EDS to identify phases and microstructural features.
Observed phenomena such as parabolic oxidation rate behavior, spinel oxide formation, internal oxidation, surface cracking, and oxide layer spallation (especially at 900 °C).
paper_reported: Oxidation kinetics in the HEA followed a parabolic rate law with a higher rate constant and increased mass gain at 900 °C compared to 700 °C.
The formation of various oxide phases (e.g., FeO, MnO, MnCr2O4, MnFe2O4, MnFeO2, and Cr2O3) depended on the oxidation time and temperature.
At 900 °C, significant oxide spallation, surface cracking, and an increase in surface roughness were observed, indicating degradation in oxidation resistance.
The oxidation mechanism was attributed to inward oxygen diffusion and outward cation transport, which ultimately led to matrix segmentation and diminished high-temperature performance.
paper_proposed: While not detailing explicit future experiments, the study implies that due to the rapid loss of oxidation resistance at 900 °C, the practical operating range of the alloy is limited (favoring applications near 700 °C).
It indirectly suggests that further work—possibly including alloy compositional tweaks (e.g., the presence of Ni to reduce cation diffusion)—could help improve high-temperature oxidation performance.

paper_did: Produced FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high‐entropy alloy powder via gas atomization.
Deposited the powder using high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying under various conditions (e.g., varying the nozzle-to-substrate distance).
Performed complementary experiments including continuous heating in air (up to 1400 °C) and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C.

Characterized the powders and coatings using optical microscopy, SEM/EDX, XRD, DTA/TGA, and microhardness tests to assess phase transformations, oxidation behavior, porosity, and mechanical properties.
paper_reported: Under HVOF spraying, in-flight oxidation causes pronounced Al diffusion from the BCC supersaturated solid solution, leading to the formation of surface alumina and a transformation of the Al-depleted BCC zones into an FCC phase.
Increasing the spraying distance increases the exposure time to oxygen, which raises the oxide (e.g., alumina) content and coating porosity, resulting in decreased microhardness.
Continuous heating in air results first in the decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma phase formation, then in oxidation and FCC appearance as Al diffuses out.

During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C, a sigma “shell” forms due to element diffusion, and although initial hardening is observed, excessive Al loss and Kirkendall porosity eventually reduce microhardness.
paper_proposed: Utilizing feedstock powder with an excessive Al concentration to prevent the undesired FCC formation during deposition.
Applying a preliminary heat treatment to the feedstock to create a protective alumina shell and enhance hardness.
Tailoring spraying parameters (such as nozzle-to-substrate distance) to optimize oxide content for targeted tribological performance at elevated temperatures.

hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in thickness is uncertain, and there is a risk that too high a velocity might adversely affect coating integrity or cause slight changes in phase formation.

paper_did: Deposited Cr‐CrₓOᵧ coatings by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) and YSZ‐CoNiCrAlY thermal barrier coating (TBC) systems (using APS for the top coat and HVOF for the bond coat) on a NiCr20Co18Ti substrate.

Performed isothermal heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h followed by long‐term oxidation at 900 °C for 1200 h, then characterized the coatings’ microstructure, oxide content, reaction layer formation, microhardness, and adhesion.

Used specifically engineered feedstock powders (e.g., milled Cr powder mixed with Ni80Cr20 and SiO₂ for the Cr-based coatings) and compared the oxidation behavior and bonding mechanisms of both coating systems.
paper_reported: The as‐sprayed Cr–CrₓOᵧ coatings contained a mix of Cr, metastable ferromagnetic CrO₂, stable Cr₂O₃ (from both primary and secondary formation), NiCr, and SiO₂ phases, and heat treatment transformed CrO₂ into stable Cr₂O₃.

Oxidation increased the oxide content from about 27% (as‐sprayed) to around 40% after heat treatment, with the formation of a homogenous thermally grown Cr₂O₃ surface layer and voids forming underneath due to diffusion phenomena (Kirkendall effect).

Interdiffusion at the coating–substrate interface led to the formation of well‐defined Cr and Ni reaction layers, and improvements in microhardness and coating cohesion were observed after heat treatment.
paper_proposed: Future work to analyze the wear and erosion behavior of the coatings in different environments.
Further laboratory investigations into the mechanisms of the metastable CrO₂ transformation and detailed oxidation kinetics to optimize coating performance.

hypotheses.intervention: Modify the combustion parameters by increasing the fuel-to-air ratio (or adjusting total gas flow) to boost particle acceleration.
hypotheses.conditions: HVAF-i7 spraying on components (including those with internal diameters as small as 120 mm) under ambient conditions, with service exposures up to 900 °C.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy leads to improved in-flight melting and splat flattening, resulting in higher mass deposition per pass and more robust inter-splat metallurgical bonding.
hypotheses.mechanism: By increasing the fuel-gas ratio, the flame energy and particle velocity are raised. This increased momentum helps particles impact the substrate with greater kinetic energy, promoting better adhesion and higher deposition efficiency. Moreover, faster particle transit reduces residence time in the flame, thereby limiting in-flight oxidation—a concern for maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A noticeable increase in coating thickness relative to the standard process with only marginal if any increase in as-sprayed oxidation, maintaining adhesion and durability in service conditions up to 900 °C.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard HVAF-i7 process parameters with a fuel-to-air mixture optimized for quality but yielding inadequate deposit thickness.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective within the operational limits of the HVAF-i7 system, provided that the increased flame energy does not induce excessive oxidation or thermal stresses; applicable for bond coats on substrates with diameters down to 120 mm.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The extent of thickness improvement is not precisely predictable because the balance between increased velocity and potential oxidation effects may vary; experimental tuning is required.

paper_did: Deposited Cr‐CrxOy coatings via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using a feedstock mixture of Cr (milled to <5 µm), Ni80Cr20 powder, and SiO2 particles onto a NiCr20Co18Ti substrate.

Deposited a conventional YSZ-CoNiCrAlY thermal barrier coating (TBC) system with an APS-sprayed 8 wt-% Y2O3-ZrO2 top coat on an HVOF-sprayed CoNi32Cr21Al8Y0.5 bond coat, and then subjected the samples to isothermal heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h followed by prolonged oxidation at 900 °C for 1200 h.

Characterized the as-sprayed, heat-treated, and oxidized states via microstructural (SEM, EDX, ImageJ analysis), chemical, and mechanical (microhardness, adhesion, crack propagation) investigations to assess oxidation behavior, diffusion-induced reaction layers, and coating integrity.
paper_reported: Heat treatment converted the metastable ferromagnetic CrO2 into stable Cr2O3 and increased the overall oxide content from about 27% to 40%, forming uniform thermally grown Cr2O3 layers that improve oxidation resistance.

The diffusion processes at the interface led to well‐defined Cr and Ni reaction layers (as explained by the Cr–Ni miscibility gap) that contributed to enhanced metallurgical bonding and substrate protection, while stress relief, sintering, and phase transformations improved microhardness and reduced crack susceptibility.
Overall, both the Cr-based system and the YSZ-CoNiCrAlY TBC were shown to protect the substrate against oxidation at 900 °C, albeit via different mechanisms.
paper_proposed: Further laboratory work to separately investigate the formation and transformation of the metastable CrO2 phase.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introduce controlled substrate pre-heating and engineered interpass dwell intervals during HVAF-i7 deposition of FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powders.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powders with a 15–45 μm size range are deposited by HVAF-i7 under ambient substrate conditions, yielding acceptable quality but inadequate coating thickness.
hypotheses.intervention: Preheat the substrate (and its near‐surface region) to an intermediate temperature (e.g., 300–500 °C) and program short dwell periods between spray passes so that the already deposited material retains heat.
hypotheses.conditions: HVAF-i7 deposition on substrates (including internal diameters down to 120 mm) under ambient pressure; service conditions up to 900 °C; dwell times and pre-heating levels are optimized to avoid overheating or unwanted phase changes.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Elevated substrate and interpass temperatures allow deposited splats to remain partially plastic and promote intersplat fusion (partial self-sintering) during the build-up, thus reducing porosity.
hypotheses.mechanism: By maintaining an elevated temperature during deposition, the thermal gradient between splats and substrate is reduced, allowing the deposited particles to achieve a modest reflow and improved metallurgical bonding. This mimics some benefits of the lengthy 900 °C heat treatment observed in the paper (PMC8541463::web::007::2_2_heat_treatment_and_oxidation) but in a rapid, layer-by-layer manner that increases deposition efficiency and thickness without a separate post-deposition process.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A statistically significant increase in overall coating thickness and improved interlamellar bonding relative to the 15–45 μm baseline, with maintained low as-sprayed oxidation and adhesion suitable for high-temperature service up to 900 °C.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard HVAF-i7 deposition using 15–45 μm feedstock on unheated substrates in continuous passes.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective so long as the pre-heating temperature is high enough to permit partial sintering without triggering unwanted phase transformations, and the dwell time is optimized for the alloy’s thermal kinetics; applicable to substrates with internal diameters as small as 120 mm.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise optimal pre-heating temperature and dwell time window need to be determined experimentally; while the direction of improved thickness is expected, the magnitude of improvement is uncertain.

The "feedstock" (coating precursor) is heated by electrical (plasma or arc) or chemical means (combustion flame). paper_did: Synthesized a CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloy by mechanically alloying high‐purity elemental powders, followed by cold pressing, sintering, and machining of consolidated samples into electrodes.
Deposited successive thin coatings on 316L stainless steel substrates using the electro spark deposition (ESD) technique under an argon atmosphere.

Characterized the coatings by SEM/EDS, XRD (revealing phase transformations – increased σ and μ phases in the coating), pull‐off adhesion tests, and corrosion resistance tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: The deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 coating exhibited a mostly homogeneous and strongly adherent layer, with a dense interfacial zone and a slightly porous upper region featuring visible splats.
XRD and microstructural analyses indicated that the rapid melting and solidification during ESD induced phase changes (e.g., formation of σ and μ phases) compared to the sintered bulk.
Corrosion testing revealed an exceptionally low corrosion rate (0.00016 mm/year) and pull‐off tests confirmed good adhesion (failure occurring in the epoxy rather than the coating–substrate bond).
paper_proposed: The paper hints at further exploring novel coating systems that can deliver long‐term resistance to high‐temperature oxidation, corrosion, and wear, and suggests that process optimization (for example, local repairs and tailored deposition on large parts) remains an important future direction.

paper_did: Produced a high‐entropy alloy (CoCrFeNiMo0.85) via mechanical alloying of high‐purity metal powders followed by pressing, sintering, and machining into electrodes.

Deposited coatings on 316L stainless steel substrates using an electro spark deposition technique under an argon atmosphere, with controlled layer thickness (25–100 µm) and tailored deposition parameters.

paper_reported: The coating exhibited a homogeneous appearance near the substrate with good adhesion (pull‐off strength up to 0.67 MPa, with failure occurring only at the epoxy interface) and minimal visible defects at the bonding region.

Corrosion tests showed an extremely low corrosion rate (0.00016 mm/year in 3.5 wt.% NaCl), validating the alloy’s potential for use in aggressive environments.
paper_proposed: The discussion hints at further optimization of coating deposition – including minimizing surface porosity and enhancing passivation – to develop advanced corrosion‐resistant coatings suitable for high‐temperature or aggressive media applications.

HVAF coating technology is the combustion of propane in a compressed air stream. Like HVOF, this produces a uniform high velocity jet. HVAF differs by including a heat baffle to further stabilize the thermal spray mechanisms. Material is injected into the air-fuel stream and coating particles are propelled toward the part. Thermal barrier coatings (TBCs) are used extensively in gas turbine engines to increase component life and engine performance. A coating of about 1-200 µm can reduce the temperature at the superalloy surface by up to 200 K. Thermal spraying techniques are coating processes in which melted (or heated) materials are sprayed onto a surface. The "feedstock" (coating precursor) is heated by electrical (plasma or arc) or chemical means (combustion flame). The bond coat is an oxidation-resistant metallic layer which is deposited directly on top of the metal substrate. It is typically 75-150 μm thick and made of a NiCrAlY or NiCoCrAlY alloy, though other bond coats made of Ni and Pt aluminides also exist. The primary purpose of the bond coat is to protect the metal substrate from oxidation and corrosion, particularly from oxygen and corrosive element

A powder mixture of metal and normal glass can be plasma-sprayed in vacuum, with a suitable composition resulting in a TBC comparable to YSZ. Additionally, metal-glass composites have superior bond-coat adherence, higher thermal expansion coefficients, and no open porosity, which prevents oxidation of the bond-coat.
